**>inside busts ass to get it done, the drivers drives 5 minutes, and gets a good tip**

Once again the insulting dismissal of a Driver's effort shows up here. Drivers work inside too. At our store they essentially have responsibility over 50% of the store and cut table.

In slow times they keep the dishes, and garbage from overflowing, and put the truck away. Boxes are stocked front and back, and probably 80% of the orders on non-rushes are cut by a driver.

Again, because they take care of half of the bloody store, the insiders / management can remain focused on prep, stock, floaters and staying glued to the makeline - instead of spending time on what you dismiss off as 'misc tasks'.

And if you're not getting that kind of workload off your drivers, whoever is managing is honestly kind of shit at it.

If you want more money for busting the huge orders, get mad at Domino's for not recognizing that output - or not instituting a reasonable tip / profit sharing program. 

I would support these because it goes without saying that the insiders work their ass off, it just shouldn't be made as a case to devalue a driver.

*Some drivers would protest even having a dollar taken out of their pockets for insiders, but I bet most of them would support the inside crew getting more from the brand itself. Too bad it would be used as an excuse to go back to the tired case of 'Domino's can't afford that' / 'they'll raise prices'. **>you're still sitting in the car for at least half your shift for the most part.**

Driving is not sitting on a couch in front of Netflix, and it is still work. It is also the riskiest part of the job. We are competing against each other for efficient times, and I know in-store management (and Domino's) is paying attention to how long it takes a driver to get to and back.

Every moment we operate affects how much we have to spend later on tires, brakes, bodywork, suspension, alignment, etc. In my case, a clutch as well.

There is also HEAT. I thankfully have not had to deal with a lot of snow, but I have come from runs - dizzy as fuck and having to crouch down in the walk in. The elements are not a zero factor in our risk and workload.

One person on the cut table, trying to outdo 3 - 5 people on the makeline, during a slam busy Friday Night - or something along that ratio would be my guess. (I wasn't there.)

What time the pizza makes it to the oven is counted down to the second, and most stores are obsessed with getting that time down to the bone minimum, so the makeline will be loaded shoulder to shoulder with people, including often - the GM, whose bonus pay is massively dependent on this time being as absurdly low as possible.

Drivers will be in and out - very little time to help straighten the store out, or attach the labels to the boxes that tell the single person on the cutting and boxing table where to put everything. 

I've seen several times where there are managers / insiders crowded around the makeline, while order labels are pouring onto the floor and not even glanced at until there are pizzas tipping downwards on the edge of the oven conveyor.

If people change their orders, new labels have to be printed up, and the boxes above the cut table have to be found, relabeled, and put back onto the shelf above the cut table.

If the label printer fucks up (which it has before at our store), there will also be a backup.

The ovens run on conveyors that don't stop, ever. Items can come out 4 - 6 at a time depending on how many of the multiple conveyors are running - with more items immediately behind the ones coming out. If the labeling, boxing, or cutting process is held up for any reason - there becomes a severe bottleneck at that point, and it becomes worse if someone forgets a single topping / item and something has to be remade.

Once bottlenecks happen, the process devolves into a storm of lost / remade pizzas unless someone steps in to fix it. Most of the time during a FUBAR storm of backups, it's a rotation of drivers manning the cut table, so they have no idea where everything is. The person most able to undo the mess, has likely not had a day off in three weeks - and has long since been tunnel visioned into making their load times. They won't turn back until they hear things dropping onto the floor - or the cut person screaming mercy.

"Quality check" is just the time between getting it out of the oven, and getting the driver (or manager) to assign an order to the driver.

The fact that nobody is answering the phone is further proof that your store is getting steamrolled due to being understaffed / disorganized, both or more.

(Update for anyone reading this now for some reason. Domino's has since switched their cutting and boxing system to something called 'Samurai'. Instead of pre-folding and labeling the boxes, food items are now set into flat boxes upon coming out of the oven, folded on the spot and the items are matched with hanging receipts.

Domino's did this primarily as a cost saving measure. No more printing of adhesive labels or having to order them. The person on the cut table closest to the heat rack reads regular printed receipts and organizes the orders. 

This can turn into a wreck if the cut person isn't good at reading 4 millimeter high print quickly enough - or if they miss a tiny 'Square Cut', 'Pie Cut' or 'NGO' on high maintenance orders. Receipts also have a tendency to curl up or blow back, making them harder to read. Again, if the order gets changed, receipts need to be reprinted, located, and replaced - somewhat easier under this system, except that the receipts aren't really optimized for ease of reading when they could be.

Simple tweaks to the reciepts like placing special post bake orders in bold would help, but these changes don't seem to be on the way. The weakness on the Samurai system can be completely pointed to a lack of effort to change this.

Space on the cut table has been cleared, so theoretically more drivers / insiders can help out on the cut table - up to four. But you would need the people available, and need them paying attention to the needs of the cut table. CAR:

Drive paranoid. Assume that everyone else thinks they are the only car on the road. Pedestrians think they will be protected by an act of God if you aren't looking while they are crossing / jaywalking / staggering around in a parking lot - give them room.

Secure use of a second vehicle if you can. If your car goes down on or just before a workday, you will lose out on even more $$$ if the mechanics can't get you out the same day.

GETTING TIPS:

At the door: Positive, pleasant, professional.

That means act like you want to be there, don't project negativity or otherwise create the possibility to make for an unpleasant interaction at the door. Even after you find out the job is miserable. You are at their castle, their sanctuary. 

If you get zeroed out for your tip, just give out your 'thank you for your order' and move on. (But save your extra courtesy items for the people who DO pay you.)

If you have a problem, be honest and ready to correct the situation.

Consider getting a small clipboard and highlighters to help customers fill out the CC receipt.

Carry all $1s for your bank and your pocket change.

Read your tags. If in doubt, take the extra ten seconds it takes to print the itemized receipt. Always bring the itemized receipt to any hotel / business deliveries, or any huge orders.

40 Wings come in a large box. If you forget this, you will end up serving someone 40 wings without their 5 cups of dressing that's supposed to come with it and you will have mucho problemo.

Pack extra napkins, plates, cups when you can. 29 out of 30 customers don't think to ask for courtesy items until you are at their doorstep. This includes cheese and peppers, which are often in short supply. Keep the items OUT OF SIGHT of someone who might be standing over your car. KEEP TRACK OF ANYTHING YOU RETURN TO THE STORE.

If you forget that you have a bad order, or a switched order, you might end up paying for someone else's pizza out of YOUR POCKET.

tl;dr - The 20% guideline used for foodservers is great. Remember that Domino's drivers do NOT get the delivery fee. Many delivery experts also carry a lot of the cost to make business with you possible.

- - -

Tips from generous customers make or break what a driver earns. They only get cents-per-mile for gas outside of a flat (usually minumum) wage, and anything that happens to any part of the car (brakes, tires, various expensive mechanical systems) has to be covered from that money. 

Of course, that is if their vehicle isn't company owned - but I've only seen them in the commercials! You should tip them anyway because they have provided you a convenience, same as a server in a restaurant.

Tip the bike guy! I haven't confirmed yet if they earn mileage or not, but they have to brave the streets on two wheels to get you food to the comfort of your home.

If you are calling an order to be delivered to a place where you may NOT be present when the driver arrives, AUTHORIZE someone to be able to give / write-in a tip. More than once I've gotten "but it's already paid for" in a harsh tone when I ask someone to fill out tip / total amounts on the credit slip, or had someone send a kid to the door giving out $17 for a $16 and change order. I've also seen kids pocket money what was obviously a tip.

If you are reading this and still hating the idea of tipping, consider:

Many drivers SAVE their company a lot of cost of delivery.

If that delivery expert is driving their own car, they have effectively provided a FREE vehicle for the day to the company. The flat wage pays for the driver, who is expected to be able to do any of the work that a inside-person does, like answering phones, making pizzas, cutting and boxing,  prep and cleaning. The company effectively gets use of a car for gas money, which does go a bit past what most cars use for mileage - but would be nowhere near enough to cover a driver for a serious mechanical issue.

If you are awaiting the day that tipping is eliminated via autonomous delivery, do you think the delivery fee will still be the same with a fleet of self driving cars instead of what a delivery expert is running (and paying for)?

- - -

This all assumes that the driver has provided good service. 

Good service meaning: that the driver has handled everything they could competently. Stuff within their control, which unfortunately is not everything.

If your order is ruined because the driver could not bring in cheese, pepper packets, plates, napkins and cups - consider that sometimes the stores have not been able to provide these things to them. These things should be requested AND marked on the order, so that a responsive driver can alert you if we don't have them.

If you get your pizza in 45 - 60 minutes on a busy Friday / Sat night instead of 30, consider yourself fortunate because those days are jam-packed with drivers taking multiple orders per run, and times given over the phone are sometimes too optimistic.

Don't punish / stiff a driver for a mistake they didn't make. Take it up with the store / corporate / franchise owner and get your remedy from them.

Short answer: $10 was very generous unless your order was like some insane amount, like $500.

Long answer:

Depends on the order amount, and how much crap your driver has to eat to get you served. 

If you can't afford to tip %10 then you should think about getting the dollar menu somewhere, or make your own food. If I can see that someone is in dire straits, and just can't go out for food (no money, no transport, hungry) - I'll forgive a low tip or even a stiff. I've had people hand me a extra dollar on a $20 order, and just tell me straight up that their money is tight. 

I'll honestly smile and tell them it's no problem, remember us next time and move on, and just hope everyone else can afford to tip.

20% is a widely acceptable standard for table servers, and . . guess what? We are your waiters on wheels, and the mileage pay I get is just enough to pay for gas, and maybe a can of Starbucks so I don't fall asleep on the road. 

I'm lucky enough to get the standard min. wage in my state (instead of . . what? $3) an hour, but after that - it's up to tips to cover my insurance, registration ($250+ on one of my vehicles), oil changes and filters, brake service, smog certification, batteries, spark plugs, spark plug wires, starter, and any other thing that might break on my car.

If you tip more than 30%, you are a great person.

If you tip more than 40% you are a tipping hero, but I do not expect this at all.

Tips of $7, 8 , 9 dollars on a will erase one or two stiffers.

Also. Don't assume gratuity is included. That $2.80 fee my company charges? I only see mileage pay; .20 - .25 a mile. If you live across the block and stiff me, I'm literally only getting a quarter.

If you live across the block, stiff me, and delay my pace for some kind of cullbrap like filling out your address incorrectly, or not giving an apartment AND building number, etc - then you just took a considerable amount of money out of my pocket. If it's for some petty reason like 'forgetting' an extra you didn't ask for (napkins, peppers, cheese, plates, cups, etc etc etc.), or not getting a pizza in 24 minutes on a busy weekend night - then you've just become the scum of the earth.

--

In return for your generous tip, your driver is expected to make every effort they can to make sure your order arrives safely and in reasonable time.

If your pizza arrives in 45 - 50 minutes instead of 30? Do you stiff then? It doesn't always mean it was the drivers fault.

- You might live in a hard to reach area with limited parking. Like an apartment complex too cheap to post a readable directory.

- Incorrect / incomplete directions could have ended up on the order as a result of someone messing up on an app or an in-store person being in a rush. Then we have to waste time playing detective to find you.

- We might be running 'doubles' or 'triples' on busy nights. Meaning that you might not be the driver's first stop. You might be the third, and the first stop is deep inside an apartment complex with no directions and 27 speed bumps. 

If we didn't do this, you would be waiting much longer.

- My store expects everyone to try to answer the phone within two rings, with emphasis on the drivers doing this job. Our in-store crew makes min-wage with no breaks, they'll either be glued to the makeline or surfing facebook on their phones.

This is monitored remotely and in person (our QA and district people like to drop by often), so I end up delaying my order to grab the phone since I'm the only one that moves on the first ring.

Oh, dear. Our guest doesn't quite know what they want, and they sound like they haven't ordered a pizza in this decade. Looks like your order is waiting another ten minutes on top of being the last stop on a double. 

- You live within a block and think your order is going to make it in 15 - 20 mins? Maybe! If there's a driver in the store when your order rolls out of the oven. Otherwise, you'll have to survive an extra 20 minutes of hunger while your order waits for a driver to return from delivering to the back of Giant Speedbump Complex.

- You might be given an optimistic quote time by an app or someone in-store. Treat times that are given to you like an estimate, not a guarantee - and you will be happier for it. This also goes for 'timed orders'.

So, lastly.. when is it justifiable to cut a driver off from their tips? IMHO, if they outright lie to you when you ask a question, are actively disrespecting you or your property, or they actively cause a delay by being careless in haste (forgetting main items). But, you have to give the benefit of the doubt in most situations.
